transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-26
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Carmen Diaz, Liam Chen (Redwood); Priya Narang, Daniel Reyes, Sofia Kline, Omar Malik (Moonbeam)

Auto Summary (auto-gen may miss stuff):
- Moonbeam evaluating open LLMs for long-context doc streaming, needs multilingual for EN/ES/DE, considering private VPC because of PII flow.
- Priority: latency < 250ms for short queries, 2-3s for multi-doc syntheses; cost target: under $0.03 per 1k tokens for production.

Transcript:
[00:00] Carmen Diaz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Carmen, I'm the AE on the account, with Liam our SE. Quick round robin?
[00:08] Priya Narang: Hi I'm Priya, CTO at Moonbeam. We're building a knowledge ingestion pipeline for customer docs and want to surface concise answers in product.
[00:14] Daniel Reyes: Daniel here, ML eng, I'll be running evals and integrating the retriever.
[00:17] Sofia Kline: Sofia, security lead, I'll focus on compliance and data flow.
[00:20] Omar Malik: Omar, product, mostly product-level success crits and latency targets.
[00:23] Carmen Diaz: Great. Quick agenda: model choice, context-length needs, tool-calling / retrievers, and deployment mode (hosted/dedicated/private). Sound ok?
[00:30] Priya Narang: Yep. Our top question is which open models to use — we prefer open models for cost and auditability, but we need good long-context behavior and multilingual support.
[00:40] Liam Chen: Right. In practice we see tradeoffs: some 8k open models are cheaper but struggle on cross-doc synthesis; 32k variants improve coherence but cost more and impact latency. Also quantization and kernels matter a lot for throughput.
[01:00] Daniel Reyes: Do you have recommendations for retriever + tool-calling pattern? We want the model to call a summarization tool and also optionally call an external search.
[01:10] Liam Chen: Yes — two patterns. 1) server-side retrieval + condensed prompt to a 32k context model; 2) hybrid: a smaller hosted model for routing + call external tool via function calling. For tool-calling we support structured tool responses — though the transcription might show "function calling" as "funct calling" in some places — but it's supported.
[01:35] Priya Narang: On security: we must keep raw docs in our VPC, and we need KMS integration for key control. Is that doable with Redwood Private?
[01:45] Carmen Diaz: Absolutely. Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. For highly regulated flows customers often pick Private or Dedicated with VPC peering. There are different levels: hosted (we handle infra), dedicated (reserved GPU pool, more isolation), private (customer control plane + VPC).
[02:05] Sofia Kline: We need SOC2 type II evidence, and ISO 27001 — can you provide docs? Also SSO via SAML is required.
[02:15] Liam Chen: Yes we can share security pack. Quick note: some of the compliance artifacts are handled by our enterprise security team; we'll route those docs.
[02:25] Omar Malik: For latency, we target sub-250ms median for single-turn QA, and under 3s for generated summaries over 10 docs. Any numbers from your side for open models?
[02:35] Liam Chen: It depends heavily on model/quantization. For example, a 13B quantized to q4_0 on A100 can do 40-60 reqs/sec at 512 tokens with 100-150ms median. 32k sequences push memory and reduce throughput; you might see 5-15 reqs/sec depending on batching. We can run benchmark with your prompts to get realistic numbers.
[03:05] Daniel Reyes: That throughput drop is worrysome — our product expects bursts. Can we burst into Dedicated capacity?
[03:15] Carmen Diaz: Yes — Dedicated has burst capacity options and autoscaling. Also smart routing can fall back from Private to Dedicated or Hosted variants if capacity hits a limit. There are policy controls.
[03:30] Priya Narang: For multilingual, we need EN, ES, DE out of box. Some open models have poor German. Do you have model catalogs with per-lang evals?
[03:40] Liam Chen: We do. We'll share a language matrix. In general, Llama-3-family variants and some Mistral derivatives perform decently, but you may need fine-tuning or instruction-tuning for German technical docs. Also be mindful of tokenizer expansion with languages like German which can increase token counts.
[04:05] Sofia Kline: On data retention: if we run hosted, will Redwood persist input documents? We need to ensure logs can be disabled and no PII retained.
[04:15] Carmen Diaz: Hosted has configurable retention; for strict PII we recommend Private where you manage storage. We also have retention flags and an enterprise contract addendum for no-persist policies.
[04:35] Omar Malik: Ok, let's talk concrete pilot. We want to understand: cost to run a 2-week pilot with 32k context on hosted vs dedicated.
[04:45] Liam Chen: We'll estimate. Quick ask: can you share expected QPS, avg tokens per request, and size of doc bundles?
[04:55] Daniel Reyes: QPS spiky — baseline 50 qps, peaks 800 qps for short bursts. Avg tokens: 120 for search QA; for syntheses up to 6k tokens. Doc bundles: typical user view pulls 20 docs of 1-3 pages each, so effective context often ~8-12k tokens if we do condensed retrieval.
[05:20] Liam Chen: That helps. For spikes, Dedicated is safer. For cost-sensitive long term, we recommend hybrid: hosted for lower volume/experiments, Dedicated for production. Private if you need on-prem KMS and VPC-only access.
[05:45] Priya Narang: Any friction integrating our retriever (we use Weaviate) with Redwood?
[05:52] Liam Chen: No major friction. We support HTTP webhook-style retriever calls and native vector store connectors for some vendors; if Weaviate isn't supported directly, the webhook pattern plus a small middleware is fine. Also consider local caching of vectors for latency.
[06:10] Daniel Reyes: The KV cache you mentioned — is that like a transformer key-value cache? We want to avoid re-encoding same context repeatedly.
[06:18] Liam Chen: It's a runtime-level KV cache for prefix contexts so repeated tokens don't get recomputed. Works well for chat sessions with repeated context. Some customers call it K-V cash in notes, so you might see that in transcriptions.
[06:35] Sofia Kline: For the security deep dive, we'll want network diagrams showing peering, ingress/egress, and proof of encryption in transit and at rest.
[06:45] Carmen Diaz: Noted — we'll bring network diagrams and KMS flow charts.
[06:52] Omar Malik: Regarding function/tool calling, we need deterministic structured outputs to map to product fields; how mature is that?
[06:58] Liam Chen: Function calling support exists; we expose structured response modes and can enforce JSON schema. Some open models are better at schema adherence; we'll test your schema in the benchmark.
[07:20] Priya Narang: Past experiences: we had hallucination issues when the retriever returned low-quality docs. Any suggestions?
[07:30] Liam Chen: Two mitigations: 1) retrieval scoring & rerank before passing to model; 2) use a verify step with a smaller fact-check model or tool to validate critical fields. Also prompt engineering helps with instruction clarity.
[07:50] Daniel Reyes: For the week-long benchmark, can you run both 8k and 32k contexts and also a pipeline where we chunk docs + use a summarizer tool?
[07:58] Liam Chen: Yes — we'll set up three arms: 8k open model, 32k open model, and 8k + toolchain (retriever + external summarizer). We'll return latency, cost per 1k tokens, rouge/qa accuracy metrics for your prompt set.
[08:20] Priya Narang: What about model rollouts? We need canary traffic (10%) then 50% then full, and an automatic fallback if quality/regression detected.
[08:30] Carmen Diaz: Redwood supports canary and A/B style rollouts with automatic regression detection tied to prompt sets/evals. If a rollout fails quality gates you can auto-fallback to previous model.
[08:42] Omar Malik: Great. Any assumptions we should flag?
[08:45] Liam Chen: Primarily: cost numbers will vary by token expansion, and any fine-tuning or instruction tuning changes costs. Also, some kernels are better on specific GPU types; we'll recommend hardware in the benchmark output.
[09:05] Sofia Kline: A nit: network egress for Private — how is that controlled? We need to avoid unexpected external leakage.
[09:12] Liam Chen: Private deployment sits inside your VPC; egress rules are under your control. We also support private endpoints and strict subnet controls. We'll show a sample VPC peering guide.
[09:30] Priya Narang: Competition — we've been talking to OpenAI for hosted, and Anthropic for safety tooling. What are differentiators?
[09:38] Carmen Diaz: We emphasize production economics and deployment flexibility — you get the same API across hosted/dedicated/private and advanced observability (token-level costs, per-route latency). Also stronger controls around on-prem KMS and audit logs for regulated customers.
[09:55] Daniel Reyes: Ok we'll send prompts and documents this week. Any blockers to starting the benchmark?
[10:02] Liam Chen: No blockers from our side — just access to the prompt set and a contact for test infra. We'll provision a short-lived sandbox account for you.
[10:14] Carmen Diaz: Quick recap before we wrap: Liam will run 3-arm benchmark (8k, 32k, 8k+toolchain) and share config; Carmen will send pricing + SLOs and security packet; Priya to share prompts and doc samples; Sofia to send security questionnaire items. We'll schedule security deep-dive for next week.
[10:35] Priya Narang: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[10:38] Omar Malik: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcript quality: Several terms transcribed inconsistently (K V cache, function calling sometimes 'funct calling', dedicated spelled 'dedicate' in one auto-summary). Natural speech markers: "uh", "like" are occasionally present but trimmed in places.
